'Rich as Croesus' - the last king of Lydia renowned for his opulence, Croesus (595-546 BCE) presided over a kingdom at the crossroads of Asia Minor, which thrived through its strategic location and natural resources, particularly gold from the Pactolus River. His reign was marked by prosperity, monumental architecture, and a reputation for philanthropy, earning him fame across the ancient world. However, Croesus’ fortunes met a dramatic turn when he misinterpreted an oracle’s prediction, leading to his defeat by Cyrus the Great of Persia, ending his reign and the Lydian kingdom's independence.

Legends abound about the origin of Croesus’ wealth, including tales of King Midas washing his golden touch into the Pactolus River and divine blessings upon Lydia. However, these mythical stories mask the true cornerstone of his riches: the revolutionary introduction of standardized gold and silver coins. Croesus is credited with minting the world’s first bi-metallic coinage, a transformative innovation that facilitated trade, stabilized the economy, and enhanced Lydia’s prominence as a commercial hub. This monetary system not only consolidated his wealth but also laid the foundation for modern economies, marking Croesus as a pivotal figure in financial history rather than merely a fabled figure of unimaginable riches.

Apollodorus of Damascus was a renowned Greek-Syrian architect and engineer of the 2nd century AD, who gained prominence as a favored architect of the Roman Emperor Trajan. Born in Damascus, Apollodorus is celebrated for his extensive contributions to Roman architecture, particularly his innovative use of concrete and his ability to integrate Greek architectural traditions with Roman engineering. Among his most famous works is Trajan's Forum, a massive public space in Rome that included the celebrated Trajan's Column, which commemorates Trajan's victory in the Dacian Wars. He also designed the monumental Trajan's Bridge over the Danube, showcasing his engineering prowess. Apollodorus' relationship with Trajan's successor, Emperor Hadrian, was less favorable, reportedly leading to his execution around AD 130 after a dispute with Hadrian. Despite this tragic end, Apollodorus of Damascus left a lasting legacy, influencing Roman architectural style and engineering techniques for generations.

Roger of Lauria (c. 1250–1305) was one of the greatest naval commanders of the Middle Ages, serving the Crown of Aragon during a period of expansion and consolidation. Born in Italy but raised in the Aragonese sphere of influence, he became the admiral of the powerful Aragonese fleet at a time when the Mediterranean was a battleground for competing Christian and Muslim powers, as well as rival European dynasties. His naval tactics, which combined strategic positioning, deception, and disciplined use of manpower, led to a series of remarkable victories against the Angevin Kingdom of Naples, the French, and the Genoese. His ability to use the advantages of galley warfare, including ramming, boarding actions, and exploiting the wind, earned him an enduring reputation as perhaps the most brilliant naval strategist of the medieval period.

Roger of Lauria’s career unfolded within the context of the Aragonese Crown’s rising power in the Mediterranean, a history often overshadowed by Castile’s later conquests in Iberia and Spanish imperial exploits. In the late 13th century, Aragon had become a formidable maritime power, ruling over Catalonia, Valencia, and the Balearic Islands, with ambitions extending into Sicily and southern Italy. This expansion was largely driven by trade, strategic marriages, and military campaigns, with the Aragonese monarchs viewing the Mediterranean as their natural sphere of influence. King Peter III of Aragon, whom Roger loyally served, launched the Sicilian Vespers campaign (1282), seizing control of Sicily from the French Angevins. This marked the beginning of Aragonese dominance in the central Mediterranean, a dominance secured and maintained largely due to Roger’s unrivaled success at sea.

While Castilian and later Spanish forces honed their battlefield skills against the Moors, developing the tactics that would culminate in the feared Tercios of the 16th century, Lauria’s mastery of naval warfare set a precedent for Spanish naval power. His innovative tactics - feigned retreats, disciplined crossbow fire from ships, and the strategic use of boarding actions - created a template for future Spanish admirals. The Aragonese expansion into the Mediterranean, secured through his victories, foreshadowed Spain’s later dominance in the Age of Exploration, when its armadas would rule the seas from the Americas to the Philippines. Though Lauria’s influence faded in his later years, and his temporary defection to the Angevins reflected the fluid loyalties of the time, his legacy endured. It is tempting to see in his unparalleled naval expertise the early stirrings of the Spanish naval tradition that would later peak with the great fleets of the Habsburgs and Bourbons, cementing Spain as a global maritime power.

Jan Žižka (c. 1360–1424) was a Bohemian military leader and a key figure in the Hussite Wars, a series of conflicts in the early 15th century centered on religious and social tensions in Bohemia. Žižka, born into the lower nobility, demonstrated exceptional military prowess and strategic acumen that earned him a reputation as one of the most creative and effective commanders of his time. One of his most remarkable achievements was adapting innovative tactics to overcome the challenges of the battlefield, including the effective use of mobile and fortified wagon forts. The armored wagons moved in trains and would circle up, forming an overlapping impromptu fortress from which they would fire their artillery baiting opposing armies into a response. The wagons could also be used in offense, charging into ranks of soldiers and knights, loaded with men firing into the groups of knights and infantry. When Zizka died, his skin was made into a drum used to summon Hussites to battle. The Hussite revolution, however, was eventually put down.

Žižka's tactics were unorthodox and innovative. He exploited geographic features to the full and maintained good discipline in his armies. He had to quickly train peasants to repeatedly face highly trained and armored opponents who usually outnumbered his own troops. For these reasons, he is often regarded as one of the greatest military commanders of all time.
Ulysses S. Grant
+1 Diplomatic Victory point.

Ulysses S. Grant (1822 – 1885). A name tied to war, to unity - one who saw a nation split in two and made it whole again. Not through words alone, not through compromise, but through the weight of iron and blood. He was not the first to lead the Union’s armies, but he was the first to see the war for what it truly was—a battle not just of men and muskets, but of industry, supply, and sheer force of will. Others before him hesitated, sought victory through maneuver alone, afraid of the cost. Grant did not flinch. He pressed forward, understanding that war, true war, is won by breaking the enemy’s ability to fight, by grinding them down until surrender is the only path left. Fort Donelson, where he demanded unconditional surrender. Shiloh, where he learned the terrible price of war but held his ground. Vicksburg, where he split the Confederacy in two, choking its lifeline along the Mississippi. And finally, in Virginia, where he bled Lee’s army dry, forcing it to retreat, to crumble, to kneel at Appomattox. Where others saw only the butcher’s toll, Grant saw the end of the war brought closer with each battle, each sacrifice.

Yet Grant was more than just a bringer of war. He understood what victory demanded, but he also knew what came after. At Appomattox, he did not revel in conquest, did not seek humiliation or retribution. He let Lee’s men keep their dignity, their horses, their lives - offering them peace instead of punishment, hoping to bind the wounds of war before they festered. As president, he carried that same vision forward, fighting to hold the Union together in a time when division still ran deep. He championed Reconstruction, not just in word, but in action, sending federal troops south to protect freedmen from the rising tide of terror—men who had once been enslaved now given rights, land, a chance to build something new. But Grant’s idealism met the reality of corruption, of political schemers and men who sought to undo what he had fought for. The Ku Klux Klan rose in the shadows, white Southern elites reclaiming their old power, and though Grant crushed them with military force for a time, the will of the nation waned. The North grew tired of war’s ghosts. Reconstruction faltered. The Union remained whole, but the dream of an America rebuilt on true equality - on the promise of the war’s sacrifices - began to slip away.

In the end, Grant walked away - not as a tyrant, not as a king, but as a man who had given everything to the nation he served. He traveled the world, meeting emperors, kings, and leaders, seeing how nations rose and fell, how power shaped the fate of people. He knew that peace was always temporary, that strength must always stand behind it. He lived long enough to see his reputation rise and fall, accused of corruption, of reckless war-making, but never once did he deny the truth of what he had done. When illness came for him, he did what he had always done - endured. Wrote his memoirs with shaking hands, determined to leave behind his own words, his own history, so that no one else would write it for him. He died not as a conqueror, not as a martyr, but as something rarer - a man who had held a nation together when it was ready to break apart, and in doing so, became a symbol of both its strength and its failures.

Andrei Dmitrievich Sakharov (1921 – 1989), was a Soviet physicist and a Nobel Peace Prize laureate, which he was awarded in 1975 for emphasizing the human rights around the world. Although he spent his career in physics during the former Soviet program of nuclear weapons overseeing the thermonuclear discharges for Russian nuclear weapons, Sakharov also did fundamental work in understanding the particle physics, magnetism, and physical cosmology. Sakaharov is mostly known for his political activism for individual freedom, human rights, civil liberties and reforms in Russia, for which, he was deemed as a dissident and faced persecution from the former Soviet establishment. The Sakharov Prize for Freedom of Thought was established in 1988 by the European Parliament in his honour, and is the highest tribute to human rights endeavours awarded by the European Union. It is awarded annually by the parliament to "those who carry the spirit of Soviet dissident Andrei Sakharov"; to "Laureates who, like Sakharov, dedicate their lives to peaceful struggle for human rights."

Michael Faraday (1791 – 1867) was an English scientist who contributed to the study of electromagnetism and electrochemistry. His main discoveries include the principles underlying electromagnetic induction, diamagnetism and electrolysis. Although Faraday received little formal education, he was one of the most influential scientists in history. It was by his research on the magnetic field around a conductor carrying a direct current that Faraday established the concept of the electromagnetic field in physics. Faraday also established that magnetism could affect rays of light and that there was an underlying relationship between the two phenomena. He similarly discovered the principles of electromagnetic induction, diamagnetism, and the laws of electrolysis. His inventions of electromagnetic rotary devices formed the foundation of electric motor technology, and it was largely due to his efforts that electricity became practical for use in technology. Albert Einstein kept a picture of Faraday on his study wall, alongside pictures of Arthur Schopenhauer and James Clerk Maxwell. Physicist Ernest Rutherford stated, "When we consider the magnitude and extent of his discoveries and their influence on the progress of science and of industry, there is no honour too great to pay to the memory of Faraday, one of the greatest scientific discoverers of all time."

Miura Anjin, known in the West as William Adams, was an English navigator who became a significant figure in early 17th-century Japan. Arriving in Japan in 1600 aboard the Dutch ship De Liefde, Adams was initially detained as a suspected pirate. However, his knowledge of navigation, shipbuilding, and Western sciences caught the attention of Tokugawa Ieyasu, who was then consolidating power as Japan's future shogun. Impressed by his abilities, Ieyasu appointed Adams as a hatamoto, a high-ranking samurai and direct vassal of the shogun. This rare honor for a foreigner reflected the trust and value Ieyasu placed in him, allowing Adams to hold lands in the Miura Peninsula, from which his Japanese name derives.

As an advisor, Miura Anjin had lasting impact through introducing European technologies and maritime strategies to Japan. His expertise in shipbuilding led to the construction of Western-style vessels, which helped Japan strengthen its naval capabilities during a period of increased maritime exploration and trade. Adams also provided insights into European geopolitics and trade dynamics, aiding Ieyasu in navigating complex relations with European powers such as the Portuguese, Spanish, and Dutch. His counsel helped shape Tokugawa policies, particularly in fostering controlled interactions with foreign merchants while protecting Japan's sovereignty.

In addition to his roles as hatamoto and advisor, Adams served as a diplomat, mediating between Japan and foreign traders. His ability to speak multiple languages, including English, Dutch, and Japanese, allowed him to act as a bridge between cultures. He facilitated trade negotiations with the Dutch East India Company and ensured Japan's advantageous position in its dealings with European powers. Despite his origins as a foreigner, Miura Anjin integrated deeply into Japanese society, earning respect for his loyalty and contributions. His life exemplifies the blending of cultures and the critical role individuals can play in shaping international relations during transformative historical periods.

Roman Fedorovich Ungern von Sternberg (aka Black Baron, Black Horseman, Mad Baron, Bloody Baron, etc., etc.; 1885-1921) was Livonian-Teutonic Buddhist, commander of the Civil War in Russia and the last dictator of Mongolia, who sought to recreate the Great Mongol Empire within the borders of the empire of Genghis Khan. In 1905, he voluntarily went to fight with Samurai in the Russo-Japanese war, and ten years later - with the Kaiser Germans in East Prussia. As soon as Nicholas II renounced the rule of this country, Ungern offered his services to Kerensky in the form of the formation of detachments from local Asians in Southern Siberia, the purpose of which would be to protect the new government from dissidents, that is, the Bolsheviks. In August 1920, instead of running to the rescue of Ataman Semenov in Primorye, decided to go to Urga (now Ulan Bator) with the two thousandth Asian Cavalry Division, which consisted of 99% of the Buryats, Tuvans , Mongols and others. In Urga, there was a Chinese garrison of 15,000 people. Despite being heavily outnumbered, Ungern prevailed. Having captured the capital of Mongolia, the baron promised its inhabitants an empire "from the Volga to the Pacific Ocean." To celebrate, Buddhist services began in the capital. The Mongolian Bogda Khan with the unpronounceable name Jebtsundamba Khutukhta declared Ungern the commander-in-chief of the Mongolian army (which did not exist in practice) and granted him the title of khan. Ungern's downfall was an attempt to march into Soviet Russia. By 1921, the White Movement was long gone, but Ungern believed that not everything was lost, and, leaving a few Buryats in Urga, he went to win back Russia from the Bolsheviks. After poking into the territory of the Soviets , the baron was forced to go back to Mongolia to prepare for a new raid. On the way back, he organized a series of executions among both captured Red Army soldiers and among his own subordinates, suspected of sympathizing with the communists. Ungern's plans were not destined to come true. In August 1921 he was betrayed and arrested by and handed over to the Soviets.

What happened later is not difficult to guess: on the personal order of Ilyich, after a six hour show trial, he was executed in Novonikolaevsk. On the night before the execution, he gnawed and ate his St. George cross so that the Bolsheviks would not get it.

Gajah Mada (loosely translated as the "Elephant General"), hero to the people of Indonesia and symbol of national pride and patriotism, served as Prime Minister of the Majapahit Empire of Indonesia for the better part of the 14th century AD. Although little information exists as to his early life and upbringing, it is known that he was born a commoner, rising to power based solely on his intellect and cunning - along with a renowned ferocity in battle. Serving as a royal bodyguard, Gajah Mada was instrumental in quashing a rebellion against his king, and was rewarded with a path to joining the ruling elite. Eventually rising to the position of Prime Minister, Gajah Mada led the Majapahit Empire to great success in conquering many of the neighboring island kingdoms, becoming the first to unite much of the territory that encompasses modern Indonesia. In modern Indonesia, Gajah Mada is viewed as a symbol of Indonesian patriotism and national pride. Gajah Mada is seen as an inspirational figure, one who exemplifies the potential greatness of all Indonesians. He would serve as a mythic propaganda symbol during the resistance to Japanese occupation and the ensuing revolt for independence from Dutch rule in the late 1940s. His legacy as the first to unite the many islands of the Indonesian archipelago into one nation will stand throughout history - as will his renowned dedication and unwavering loyalty to his king and the Majapahit people.

Peter Carl Fabergé, also known as Karl Gustavovich Fabergé was a Russian jeweller best known for the famous Fabergé eggs made in the style of genuine Easter eggs, but using precious metals and gemstones rather than more mundane materials. He was one of the sons of the founder of the famous jewelry legacy House of Fabergé - In 1916, the House of Fabergé became a joint-stock company with a capital of 3 million rubles. The following year upon the outbreak of the October Revolution, the business was taken over by a 'Committee of the Employees of the Company K Fabergé'. In 1918 The House of Fabergé was seized by the Bolsheviks. In early October the stock was confiscated. The House of Fabergé was no more. After the nationalisation of the business, Carl Fabergé left St. Petersburg on the last diplomatic train for Riga. In mid-November, the Revolution having reached Latvia, he fled to Germany and first settled in Bad Homburg and then in Wiesbaden. Eugène, the Fabergés' eldest, travelled with his mother in darkness by sleigh and on foot through snow-covered woods and reached Finland in December 1918. During June 1920, Eugène reached Wiesbaden and accompanied his father to Switzerland where other members of the family had taken refuge at the Bellevue Hotel in Pully, near Lausanne. He died in Switzerland on September 24, 1920. His family believed he died of a broken heart. Although today the House of Fabergé is famed for its Imperial Easter eggs, it made many more objects ranging from silver tableware to fine jewelry which were also of exceptional quality and beauty, and until its departure from Russia during the revolution, Fabergé's company became the largest jewelry business in the country. In addition to its Saint Petersburg headquarters, it had branches in Moscow, Odessa, Kiev and London. It produced some 150,000 to 200,000 objects from 1882 until 1917.

Charles XII of Sweden, born in 1682, ascended to the throne in 1697 at the young age of 15. His reign, known as the Age of Liberty, was marked by extraordinary military prowess and significant reforms. Charles XII is often regarded as a military genius and has been dubbed the "God of War" for his exceptional leadership on the battlefield. His military reforms transformed the Swedish army into a highly disciplined and effective force. During the Great Northern War (1700-1721), Charles XII exhibited remarkable strategic brilliance, achieving victories against numerically superior foes. His daring tactics and audacious campaigns, such as the invasion of Russia, showcased his unparalleled military acumen. However, his aggressive approach eventually led to the decline of the Swedish Empire, especially after the disastrous Battle of Poltava in 1709. Despite his later defeats and exile, Charles XII remains a legendary figure in military history for his innovative reforms and unparalleled prowess on the battlefield.

30 years before Vasco da Gama's famous journey, a Russian merchant from Tver - Afanasy Nikitin - voyaged to India and described his trip in a narrative known as The Journey Beyond Three Seas. In 1466 Nikitin left his hometown of Tver on a commercial trip to India. He travelled down the Volga River, and although Tatars attacked and robbed him near Astrakhan, he succeeded in reaching Derbent, where he joined Vasili Papin, the envoy of Ivan the Great (the Grand Prince of All Rus') to the shah of Shirvan. At Derbent, Nikitin vainly endeavoured to find means of returning to Russia; failing in this, he went on to Baku and later to Persia proper by crossing the Caspian Sea. He lived in Persia for one year. In the spring of 1469, Nikitin arrived at the city of Ormus and then, crossing the Arabian Sea, and making several prolonged stays along the way, reached the sultanate of Bahmani, where he would live for three years. From what he tells us, he appears to have made his living by horse-dealing. During that time he visited the Hindu sanctuary of Perwattum, which he called "the Jerusalem of the Hindus". On his way back, Nikitin visited Muscat, the Arabian sultanate of Somalia, and Trabzon. In 1472 he arrived at Feodosiya by crossing the Black Sea. On his way to Tver, Nikitin died not far from Smolensk in the autumn of that year. During his trip, Nikitin studied the population of India, its social system, government, military (he witnessed war-games featuring war elephants), its economy, religion, lifestyles, and natural resources. The abundance and trustworthiness of Nikitin's factual material provide a valuable source of information about India at that time, and his remarks on the trade of Hormuz, Cambay, Calicut, Dabhol, Ceylon, Pegu and China; on royal progresses and other functions, both ecclesiastical and civil, at Bahmani, and on the wonders of the great fair at Perwattum—as well as his comparisons of things Russian and Indian—deserve special notice.
Lawrence of Arabia

Thomas Edward Lawrence (16 August 1888 – 19 May 1935) was a British archaeologist, army officer, diplomat, and writer who became renowned for his role in the Arab Revolt (1916–1918) and the Sinai and Palestine Campaign (1915–1918) against the Ottoman Empire during the First World War. The breadth and variety of his activities and associations, and his ability to describe them vividly in writing, earned him international fame as Lawrence of Arabia, a title used for the 1962 film based on his wartime activities. In 1916, he travelled to Mesopotamia and to Arabia on intelligence missions and became involved with the Arab Revolt as a liaison to the Arab forces, along with other British officers, supporting the Arab Kingdom of Hejaz's independence war against its former overlord, the Ottoman Empire. He worked closely with Emir Faisal, a leader of the revolt, and he participated, sometimes as leader, in military actions against the Ottoman armed forces, culminating in the capture of Damascus in October 1918. Lawrence was instrumental in establishing a provisional Arab government under Faisal in newly liberated Damascus, which he had envisioned as the capital of an Arab state. Faisal's rule as king, however, came to an abrupt end in 1920, after the battle of Maysaloun when the French Forces of General Henri Gouraud entered Damascus under the command of General Mariano Goybet, destroying Lawrence's dream of an independent Arabia. King George V offered Lawrence a knighthood on 30 October 1918 at a private audience in Buckingham Palace for his services in the Arab Revolt, but he declined. He was unwilling to accept the honour in light of how his country had betrayed the Arabs.

Cecil Rhodes, born in 1853 in England, embarked on a journey to wealth that began when he traveled to South Africa at the age of 17. Initially sent for health reasons, Rhodes was captivated by the opportunities in the booming diamond fields of Kimberley. Using borrowed money, he invested in diamond claims, eventually founding the De Beers Mining Company in 1888. Through strategic acquisitions and partnerships, he consolidated the diamond industry under his control, making De Beers a global powerhouse. Simultaneously, he pursued education at Oxford, albeit intermittently, blending his academic pursuits with his business ambitions in South Africa.

Rhodes’s wealth grew to staggering proportions, fueled by his dominance in diamonds and later ventures in gold mining. De Beers, under his leadership, controlled 90% of the world’s diamond production at its peak. This near-monopoly allowed Rhodes to amass immense personal wealth and exert significant political and economic influence. His financial success enabled him to become Prime Minister of the Cape Colony from 1890 to 1896, during which he implemented policies aimed at expanding British imperial dominance. His wealth and power were emblematic of the exploitative colonial economies that enriched European elites while marginalizing native populations.

Rhodes’s legacy is deeply polarizing. On one hand, his endowment established the prestigious Rhodes Scholarship, fostering international education and intellectual exchange. However, his imperialist ambitions and policies left a far darker mark. Rhodes was a fervent advocate of British colonial expansion, epitomized by his dream of a “Cape to Cairo” railway. He played a pivotal role in the establishment of Rhodesia (modern-day Zimbabwe and Zambia), a territory named in his honor, which became synonymous with racial segregation and white minority rule. His policies disenfranchised and dispossessed African populations, laying the groundwork for systemic inequality and conflict. Today, Rhodes is remembered as both a visionary benefactor and a symbol of colonial exploitation and racial oppression, making his legacy one of profound complexity and controversy.

Orban, also known as Urban (Hungarian: Orbán; died 1453), was an iron founder and engineer from Brassó, Transylvania, in the Kingdom of Hungary (today Brașov, Romania), who cast large-calibre artillery for the Ottoman siege of Constantinople in 1453. He had offered his services to the Byzantines in 1452, a year before the Ottomans attacked the city, but the Byzantine emperor Constantine XI could not afford Orban's high salary nor did the Byzantines possess the materials necessary for constructing such a large siege cannon. Orban then left Constantinople and approached the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II, who was preparing to besiege the city. Claiming that his weapon could blast 'the walls of Babylon itself', Orban was given abundant funds and materials by the sultan. Orban managed to build the giant gun within three months at Adrianople, whence sixty oxen dragged it to Constantinople. Orban also produced other, smaller cannons used by the Turkish siege forces. Guns of Urban helped the Turks conquer the City of the World's Desire and set an important stepping stone in further expansion of Ottoman Empire.

Agrippa, whose full name was Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa, was a prominent Roman statesman and military general during the reign of Emperor Augustus in the 1st century BCE. Born in 63 BCE, Agrippa played a crucial role in the rise of Augustus to power and the establishment of the Roman Empire. His military prowess was evident in his leadership during several key naval battles, most notably the Battle of Actium in 31 BCE, where he decisively defeated the forces of Mark Antony and Cleopatra. Agrippa's strategic acumen and naval expertise were instrumental in securing Augustus's victory and consolidating Roman control over the Mediterranean. In addition to his military achievements, Agrippa was also known for his architectural and engineering talents. He earned a reputation as a wonder constructor for his involvement in various building projects throughout the Roman Empire. One of his most famous contributions was the construction of the Pantheon in Rome, a remarkable architectural marvel known for its iconic dome. Agrippa's legacy as both a skilled naval commander and a visionary builder left an indelible mark on Roman history, solidifying his place as one of the key figures of the Augustan Age.

Michiel de Ruyter (1607–1676) was one of the greatest naval commanders in Dutch history and a key figure in the 17th-century Dutch Golden Age. Born in Vlissingen, he rose from humble beginnings to become the Lieutenant Admiral of the Dutch Republic, leading the Dutch fleet in numerous conflicts against England, France, and other European powers. De Ruyter was renowned for his tactical brilliance, courage, and leadership, making him a national hero whose legacy continues to be celebrated in the Netherlands. Statues, street names, and even naval ships bear his name, reflecting his deep imprint on Dutch cultural identity.

De Ruyter's naval victories were crucial in maintaining Dutch independence and securing the Republic's economic dominance in Europe. His most famous achievement was the Raid on the Medway (1667) during the Second Anglo-Dutch War, in which he led a daring assault up the River Thames, capturing or destroying much of the English fleet and humiliating England. He also played a key role in the Third Anglo-Dutch War, where he successfully defended the Republic in the battles of Solebay (1672) and Texel (1673) against an Anglo-French alliance. His ability to command smaller, well-coordinated fleets against numerically superior enemies solidified his reputation as one of history’s greatest admirals.

Beyond his naval battles, De Ruyter contributed significantly to the defense of the Netherlands, particularly through coastal fortifications and water-based defensive strategies. The Dutch Waterline, a series of flooded areas designed to halt invading armies, was a crucial element in Dutch military planning. Though the concept predated him, De Ruyter’s expertise in naval defense and maritime strategy influenced its development. His experiences defending the coastline against English and French incursions reinforced the importance of naval power in protecting Dutch sovereignty. His leadership helped shape Dutch maritime defenses, ensuring that the Netherlands remained a formidable naval power well into the 18th century.

Muhammad V (r. 1354–1359, 1362–1391) was one of the most influential rulers of the Nasrid Dynasty, leaving an indelible mark on the cultural and architectural heritage of Al-Andalus. His reign was a period of artistic flourishing, during which the Alhambra reached the peak of its grandeur. Muhammad V inherited the palace complex from his father, Yusuf I, who had already begun transforming it into a center of power and refinement. However, it was under Muhammad V’s rule that the Alhambra was elevated to a masterpiece of Islamic architecture, blending Moorish, Andalusian, and Persian influences with remarkable sophistication. His architectural vision was not merely about decoration; it was about creating a harmonious fusion of light, space, and water, symbolizing both power and serenity.

One of Muhammad V’s most defining contributions to the Alhambra was the construction of the Palace of the Lions, which remains one of the most breathtaking examples of Islamic art and engineering. The palace is centered around the Court of the Lions, a courtyard featuring a striking white marble fountain supported by twelve intricately sculpted lions—a rare example of animal representation in Islamic art, suggesting the influence of earlier Hispano-Moorish traditions. The surrounding arcades, delicate stucco work, and honeycomb muqarnas vaults create an ethereal effect, emphasizing balance and elegance. The Hall of the Two Sisters and the Hall of the Abencerrajes, both located within the palace, exemplify Muhammad V’s commitment to craftsmanship, with their intricate geometrical patterns, Arabic calligraphy, and domed ceilings designed to evoke the celestial realm. His patronage extended beyond the Alhambra, as he also commissioned the Maristan of Granada, a sophisticated hospital complex, and oversaw the expansion of urban infrastructure in the city.

Muhammad V’s reign was not only a period of artistic achievement but also one of diplomatic and cultural exchange, which deeply influenced the development of Nasrid art. He maintained close relations with the Christian Kingdom of Castile and, for a time, was on friendly terms with Pedro I of Castile (Pedro the Cruel), which allowed for the exchange of artistic techniques and ideas. Some historians believe that Muhammad V’s architectural style may have influenced the Mudéjar art found in Spanish Christian palaces, including parts of the Alcázar of Seville. His ability to integrate various artistic traditions while maintaining a distinctly Islamic identity in his constructions is what makes his legacy so extraordinary. Under his rule, the Alhambra became not just a fortress or a royal residence, but a symbol of the height of Nasrid civilization, where art, poetry, and science flourished alongside political power. His vision and artistic patronage secured the Alhambra’s status as one of the greatest architectural wonders of the medieval world.

Avicenna's contributions laid foundational principles in the medical field, such as the concept of contagion and the importance of clinical trials. His integration of Aristotle's philosophy with Islamic thought and his development of early scientific methods greatly influenced the development of science and medicine.

Avicenna's scientific contributions significantly influenced Muslim theology, particularly in how knowledge and reason were perceived within the Islamic intellectual tradition. By merging Aristotelian philosophy with Islamic teachings, Avicenna helped to create a philosophical framework that emphasized the harmony between reason and faith. His works provided theological arguments for the existence of God based on logic and empirical observations, which were particularly appealing to Muslim philosophers who sought to reconcile faith with the scientific knowledge of their time. Furthermore, Avicenna's emphasis on the soul's immortality and his exploration of metaphysical concepts offered profound insights that enriched Islamic mystical thought, paving the way for later scholars like Al-Ghazali and Averroes. Through his integration of science and theology, Avicenna played a crucial role in shaping Islamic philosophy, demonstrating that scientific inquiry and religious belief could coexist and even complement each other.

Friedrich Nietzsche (1844–1900) was a German philosopher and cultural critic who published intensively in the 1870s and 1880s. He is famous for uncompromising criticisms of traditional European morality and religion, as well as of conventional philosophical ideas and social and political pieties associated with modernity. Nietzsche's writing spans philosophical polemics, poetry, cultural criticism, and fiction while displaying a fondness for aphorism and irony. Prominent elements of his philosophy include his radical critique of truth in favor of perspectivism; a genealogical critique of religion and Christian morality and related theory of master–slave morality; the aesthetic affirmation of existence in response to the "death of God" and the profound crisis of nihilism; the notion of Apollonian and Dionysian forces; and a characterization of the human subject as the expression of competing wills, collectively understood as the will to power.

Jacob Kettler, Duke of Kurland and Semigallia (1610–1682), stands as one of the most remarkable yet often overlooked figures of 17th-century European mercantilism. He embodied the very essence of a "Merchant Lord," blending aristocratic governance with an ambitious and highly pragmatic approach to commerce and colonial expansion. Educated in the courts of Western Europe, particularly the Netherlands and England, Kettler absorbed the principles of mercantilism and state-driven commerce, which he would later apply in transforming Kurland into a maritime power. Under his rule, the Duchy, despite its modest size, emerged as a significant player in the Northern European trade networks. He aggressively expanded Kurland’s merchant fleet, developed shipbuilding industries, and modernized ports to facilitate exports of timber, hemp, and tar - essential resources for European naval powers. Unlike other rulers of his time, Kettler understood that wealth was not merely tied to land but could be derived from strategic maritime dominance and shrewd investment in trade routes. His policies transformed Kurland into a hub of commerce, allowing it to punch well above its weight in the geopolitical arena.

Kettler's ambitions extended far beyond the shores of the Baltic. In a bold and unusual move for a minor European state, he embarked on colonial ventures, seeking to secure overseas territories that would serve as sources of raw materials and strategic trade outposts. He established colonies in Tobago in the Caribbean and the island of St. Andrews (now known as Kunta Kinteh Island) in the Gambia. These colonies were meant to supply Kurland with exotic goods, including sugar, tobacco, spices, and, more controversially, slaves. His efforts reflected an early understanding of the transatlantic economy, in which controlling trade routes and commodities was as important as military might. However, Kettler’s colonial ventures were repeatedly undermined by larger European powers, particularly the Dutch and the English, who saw Kurland’s expansion as an infringement on their commercial interests. Despite these setbacks, his vision of a Baltic-based maritime empire remained a testament to his ingenuity and boldness, proving that even small duchies could compete in the high-stakes game of global commerce.

Perhaps the most audacious of Kettler’s ideas was his far-fetched aspiration to colonize Australia - a plan that would have placed Kurland at the forefront of European exploration in the Pacific over a century before the British arrived. While there is little evidence that Kurland ever launched an actual expedition to Australia, records suggest that Kettler saw the largely unknown southern continent as the ultimate frontier for expansion. His vision likely stemmed from the Dutch discoveries of the Australian coast in the early 1600s, which suggested the presence of untapped resources and strategic trade potential. Had he succeeded, Kurland - a small Baltic duchy - might have altered the course of global history, creating an unlikely colonial empire in the Southern Hemisphere. Though it remains one of the more eccentric and implausible aspects of his legacy, it encapsulates the boundless ambition and commercial zeal that defined his rule. Kettler’s relentless drive to expand trade, acquire colonies, and transform his duchy into a maritime power makes him one of the most intriguing merchant rulers of early modern Europe.

His innovative approach to landscape design emphasized naturalistic features, sweeping lawns, and strategically placed bodies of water, departing from the more formal and structured designs of earlier garden styles. One of Brown's key contributions was his ability to seamlessly integrate the natural and man-made elements of a landscape, creating a harmonious and picturesque environment. His landscapes were characterized by undulating lawns, strategically placed clumps of trees, and serpentine lakes that gave the illusion of natural spontaneity. Brown's skill in manipulating the topography and vegetation allowed him to transform the appearance of vast estates, earning him commissions from influential landowners and aristocrats across England. His work is often associated with the concept of the "English landscape garden," and he is credited with shaping the aesthetic preferences of his time. Brown's landscapes were not just visually appealing but also aimed at evoking a sense of tranquility and contemplation, emphasizing the beauty of the natural world. His impact on the field of landscape architecture is enduring, and many of his creations remain cherished examples of the picturesque landscape style.

He introduced the concept of the "French Formal Garden," characterized by grand axial perspectives, meticulously manicured lawns, intricate parterre de broderie (embroidery-style flowerbeds), and elaborate water features. The Gardens of Versailles, particularly the iconic Hall of Mirrors parterre and the impressive Grand Canal, exemplify his mastery in creating harmonious landscapes. Le Nôtre's ability to manipulate the natural terrain, his use of perspective, and his skillful management of water elements set a standard for formal garden design across Europe. His legacy extended beyond Versailles, influencing generations of landscape architects and leaving an indelible mark on the history of garden design. The Gardens of Versailles remain a testament to Le Nôtre's artistic vision and continue to attract visitors from around the world.

Ibn Battuta (24 February 1304 – 1368/1369) was a Muslim Berber-Moroccan scholar, jurist and explorer who widely travelled the Old World, largely in the lands of Dar al-Islam, travelling more than any other explorer in pre-modern history, totalling around 117,000 km (72,000 miles), surpassing Zheng He with about 50,000 km (30,000 miles) and Marco Polo with 24,000 km (15,000 miles). Over a period of thirty years, Ibn Battuta visited most of the Old World, including Central Asia, Southeast Asia, South Asia, China and the Iberian Peninsula. His Rihlah, as his book is commonly known, is an important document shedding light on many aspects of the social, cultural, and political history of a great part of the Muslim world. Ibn Battuta was a curious observer interested in the ways of life in various countries, and he described his experiences with a human approach rarely encountered in official historiography. Another interesting aspect of the Riḥlah is the gradual revealing of the character of Ibn Battuta himself; in the course of the narrative the reader may learn the opinions and reactions of an average middle-class Muslim of the 14th century. He was deeply rooted in orthodox Islam but, like many of his contemporaries, oscillated between the pursuit of its legislative formalism and an adherence to the mystic path and succeeded in combining both. He did not offer any profound philosophy but accepted life as it came to him, leaving to posterity a true picture of himself and his times.

He is best known to the general public for his invention of the technique of treating milk and wine to stop bacterial contamination, a process now called pasteurization. Pasteur also made significant discoveries in chemistry, most notably on the molecular basis for the asymmetry of certain crystals and racemization. Early in his career, his investigation of tartaric acid resulted in the first resolution of what is now called optical isomerism. His work led the way to the current understanding of a fundamental principle in the structure of organic compounds.

Hugo Grotius, born on April 10, 1583, in Delft, Netherlands, is often hailed as the "father of international law." His seminal work, De Jure Belli ac Pacis (On the Law of War and Peace), published in 1625, laid the foundations for modern international legal principles. Grotius was a prodigious scholar and lawyer who developed his ideas during a period of intense religious and political conflict in Europe, including the Thirty Years' War. His writings emphasized the natural law theory, which posits that certain rights are inherent to all human beings, independent of laws or customs of specific societies. Grotius argued that states are bound by the same moral laws that govern individuals, advocating for the restraint of war and the establishment of a framework for peace and justice based on reason and natural law. His work influenced the development of the concept of just war and the laws governing the conduct of war and peace.

Grotius's ideas on international cooperation were revolutionary because they transcended the prevailing notions of absolute sovereignty and religiously justified conflicts. By advocating for universal principles that could govern relations between different states and cultures, Grotius laid the groundwork for what would eventually become the modern system of international relations and organizations like the United Nations. His vision of a world governed by laws rather than brute force resonated through the centuries, influencing thinkers like John Locke, Immanuel Kant, and the framers of the U.S. Constitution. Grotius's belief in the power of law and reason as tools for resolving international conflicts marked a critical step in the journey toward a more peaceful and cooperative global community. His legacy endures in the field of international law and the ongoing quest for a just and peaceful world order.

Mahbub ul Haq, born on February 24, 1934, in Jammu, British India (now part of Pakistan), was a prominent Pakistani economist and visionary who made groundbreaking contributions to the field of development economics. After obtaining his Ph.D. in economics from Yale University and serving at institutions like the World Bank, Haq's experiences shaped his views on economic growth and development. In response, Haq introduced the Human Development Index (HDI) in 1990, a composite measure that considers life expectancy, education, and per capita income, shifting the focus from purely economic growth to the overall well-being and capabilities of individuals.

Throughout his career, Mahbub ul Haq advocated for policies and initiatives that aimed at poverty alleviation, equitable access to education, and healthcare, emphasizing that real progress is measured by improvements in people's quality of life. As a Special Advisor to the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), he played a key role in initiating the annual Human Development Report, which has since become a crucial tool for policymakers worldwide. Haq's work fundamentally altered the discourse on international development, moving the conversation from economic indicators to human-centered measures of progress. His ideas not only influenced global development policies but also inspired the broader movement towards sustainable development goals that prioritize human rights, equality, and dignity. Mahbub ul Haq's legacy continues to inspire economists, policymakers, and international organizations in their quest to create a more just and humane world.

Robert Schuman, born on June 29, 1886, in Luxembourg City, Luxembourg, was a French statesman whose vision for peace and unity in post-war Europe laid the groundwork for what would eventually become the European Union. Schuman's early life, marked by the shifting borders of Europe, gave him a deep understanding of the Franco-German conflict that had fueled two world wars. After World War II, as French Foreign Minister, Schuman sought to prevent future conflicts by fostering cooperation between historic adversaries, particularly France and Germany. On May 9, 1950, Schuman presented the Schuman Declaration, proposing that France and Germany pool their coal and steel production under a common High Authority, open to other European countries. This proposal aimed to make war between France and Germany not only unthinkable but materially impossible by binding their economies together. The Schuman Declaration is widely regarded as the beginning of the European integration process, leading to the creation of the European Coal and Steel Community (ECSC) in 1951.

Schuman's vision extended beyond economic cooperation; he believed that a united Europe was essential for maintaining lasting peace and stability. He saw European integration as a means to foster democracy, uphold human rights, and promote economic prosperity. His efforts led to the establishment of key European institutions and set the stage for the Treaty of Rome in 1957, which created the European Economic Community (EEC), the precursor to today's European Union. Schuman's dedication to peace and unity earned him the title of one of the "founding fathers of Europe," alongside figures like Jean Monnet and Konrad Adenauer. His legacy is celebrated annually on May 9, known as Europe Day, which commemorates the Schuman Declaration and honors his enduring commitment to a peaceful and united Europe. Through his work, Robert Schuman demonstrated the power of collaboration and diplomacy in overcoming deep-rooted divisions, paving the way for a new era of European cooperation and integration.

François-Marie Arouet, better known by his pen name Voltaire, was born on November 21, 1694, in Paris, France. He emerged as one of the most influential writers and philosophers of the Enlightenment era, known for his wit, criticism of established institutions, and advocacy for civil liberties. Voltaire's works, including his famous novel Candide, were characterized by a sharp critique of religious dogma, superstition, and the authoritarianism of both church and state. Through his essays, plays, and letters, Voltaire championed freedom of speech, freedom of religion, and the separation of church and state. His incisive commentary often put him at odds with the authorities, leading to periods of imprisonment and exile. Nevertheless, Voltaire's relentless pursuit of truth and justice earned him a reputation as a defender of the oppressed and a critic of tyranny.

Voltaire's contributions to ideas of peace and international cooperation are evident in his promotion of tolerance and reason as foundations for a harmonious society. He was deeply affected by events such as the execution of the Protestant Jean Calas, whom Voltaire defended vehemently, exposing the miscarriage of justice motivated by religious intolerance. His advocacy helped to clear Calas's name posthumously and highlighted the need for a fair judicial system. Voltaire's writings inspired the Enlightenment movement across Europe, encouraging intellectuals and political leaders to challenge the status quo and seek reforms that would promote human rights and the betterment of society. His belief in the power of reason and his fight against fanaticism and intolerance laid the groundwork for modern secular and humanistic ideals, contributing significantly to the shaping of democratic principles and the pursuit of a more just and peaceful world.

Jean-Jacques Rousseau, born on June 28, 1712, in Geneva, Switzerland, was a profound philosopher whose ideas significantly influenced the intellectual landscape of the Enlightenment and the subsequent political developments in Europe. Rousseau's most notable works, including The Social Contract and Emile, or On Education, articulated his thoughts on human nature, society, and the ideal forms of government. He challenged the prevailing belief in the inherent superiority of civilized society over the natural state, arguing that humans were fundamentally good in their natural state but corrupted by the institutions and inequalities of society. In The Social Contract, Rousseau introduced the revolutionary idea that legitimate political authority arises from a social contract agreed upon by all citizens for their collective well-being. He famously asserted that "Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains," highlighting the need for a political order based on popular sovereignty and general will, where individuals could achieve true freedom by participating directly in the formation of laws and policies.

Rousseau's ideas had a profound impact on the development of democratic thought and the concept of individual rights, influencing both the American and French Revolutions. His vision of a society based on equality, freedom, and mutual respect challenged the existing monarchical and hierarchical structures, advocating for a government that reflected the common interests of its people. Rousseau also emphasized education's role in nurturing the natural goodness of humans, arguing for a system that developed individuals' moral and intellectual capacities rather than imposing rigid societal norms. His thoughts on liberty, equality, and the importance of civic participation laid the foundations for modern democratic ideals and continue to resonate in contemporary debates about governance, justice, and human rights. Through his writings, Rousseau became a crucial figure in the Enlightenment, inspiring generations to seek a more just, equitable, and peaceful society.

He was virtually unknown during his lifetime and was almost exclusively published in pulp magazines before he died in poverty at the age of 46, but is now regarded as one of the most significant 20th-century authors of supernatural horror fiction. Among his most celebrated tales are "The Call of Cthulhu", "The Rats in the Walls", At the Mountains of Madness, The Shadow over Innsmouth, and The Shadow Out of Time. His writings form the basis of the Cthulhu Mythos, which has inspired a large body of pastiches across several mediums drawing on Lovecraft's characters, setting and themes, constituting a wider subgenre known as Lovecraftian horror.

From the age of nine he dreamed of becoming a writer of adventure fiction but did not have real success until he was 23. Thereafter, until his death by suicide at age 30, Howard's writings were published in a wide selection of magazines, journals, and newspapers, and he became proficient in several subgenres. The main outlet for his stories was Weird Tales, where Howard created Conan the Barbarian. With Conan and his other heroes, Howard helped fashion the genre now known as sword and sorcery, spawning many imitators and giving him a large influence in the fantasy field. Howard remains a highly read author, with his best works still reprinted, and is one of the best-selling fantasy writers of all time.

Sébastien Le Prestre de Vauban (1633–1707) was a French military engineer, strategist, and Marshal of France who revolutionized fortress design and siege warfare during the reign of King Louis XIV. Born into a modest noble family in Saint-Léger-de-Foucheret, Vauban's early exposure to military life began when he joined the army of the rebellious Fronde against royal authority. However, he soon switched allegiance to the monarchy and entered the service of Cardinal Mazarin. Recognized for his technical expertise, Vauban quickly rose through the ranks, earning the trust of Louis XIV. Throughout his career, he supervised the construction or renovation of over 160 fortresses across France, designing an extensive network of defensive structures known as the Pré Carré (or "Double Line"), which safeguarded France’s frontiers. His innovations in fortification combined geometry, artillery science, and strategic planning, creating bastions and star forts that enhanced defensive capabilities while making sieges more methodical and scientific.

Vauban's expertise extended beyond fortifications; he also developed systematic siege tactics that emphasized engineering precision and minimal casualties. His "siege parallels" method involved a progressive approach to enemy fortifications through successive trenches, reducing risks for attacking forces and increasing efficiency. This strategy became the standard for European warfare for over a century. His reforms were not limited to military matters—Vauban also advocated for economic and social improvements, including fairer taxation policies to lessen the burden on commoners. Despite his service to the crown, his progressive ideas sometimes conflicted with royal policies. In his later years, he was marginalized for his views on tax reform but remained a respected figure in military engineering. Vauban’s legacy endures through the numerous fortresses he built, many of which are now UNESCO World Heritage sites, and through his lasting influence on military strategy and engineering.

His refined process made paper more accessible and practical for everyday use, which had a transformative impact on communication, record-keeping, and cultural development in China.

The widespread adoption of Cai Lun's papermaking technique resulted in significant economic benefits for Chinese papermakers. By providing a more cost-effective and efficient medium for writing, paper became a highly sought-after commodity, both domestically and internationally. As a result, paper production became a lucrative industry in China, with papermakers enjoying great profits. The affordability and practicality of paper spurred a boom in literacy and scholarly activity, further driving demand. Moreover, as the knowledge of papermaking spread along the Silk Road, it became a valuable export, enhancing trade relations and China's economic influence. Cai Lun's innovation thus laid the foundation for the proliferation of paper-based communication and record-keeping, which would eventually spread across the world, profoundly impacting global civilization.

Also known as Shen Gua, courtesy name Cunzhong and pseudonym Mengqi (now usually given as Mengxi) Weng, he was a Chinese polymathic scientist and statesman of the Song dynasty. Excelling in many fields of study and statecraft, he was a mathematician, astronomer, meteorologist, geologist, entomologist, anatomist, climatologist, zoologist, botanist, pharmacologist, medical scientist, agronomist, archaeologist, ethnographer, cartographer, geographer, geophysicist, mineralogist, encyclopedist, military general, diplomat, hydraulic engineer, inventor, economist, academy chancellor, finance minister, governmental state inspector, philosopher, art critic, poet, and musician. He was the head official for the Bureau of Astronomy in the Song court, as well as an Assistant Minister of Imperial Hospitality. At court his political allegiance was to the Reformist faction known as the New Policies Group, headed by Chancellor Wang Anshi. Alongside his colleague Wei Pu, Shen planned to map the orbital paths of the Moon and the planets in an intensive five-year project involving daily observations, yet this was thwarted by political opponents at court. To aid his work in astronomy, Shen Kuo made improved designs of the armillary sphere, gnomon, sighting tube, and invented a new type of inflow water clock. Shen Kuo devised a geological hypothesis for land formation (geomorphology), based upon findings of inland marine fossils, knowledge of soil erosion, and the deposition of silt. He also proposed a hypothesis of gradual climate change, after observing ancient petrified bamboos that were preserved underground in a dry northern habitat that would not support bamboo growth in his time. He was the first literary figure in China to mention the use of the drydock to repair boats suspended out of water, and also wrote of the effectiveness of the relatively new invention of the canal pound lock. Chinese philosopher Mozi so far is the first person in history to describe camera obscura (a basic camera). Shen implemented an improved version of the camera, nearly 2000 years later. Shen wrote extensively about movable type printing invented by Bi Sheng, and because of his written works the legacy of Bi Sheng and the modern understanding of the earliest movable type has been handed down to later generations. Following an old tradition in China, Shen created a raised-relief map while inspecting borderlands. Khalid ibn al-Walid ibn al-Mughira al-Makhzumi (died 642) was a 7th-century Arab military commander. He initially headed campaigns against Muhammad on behalf of the Quraysh. He later became a Muslim and spent the remainder of his career in service to Muhammad and the first two Rashidun caliphs: Abu Bakr and Umar. Islamic tradition credits Khalid for his battlefield tactics and effective leadership of the early Muslim conquests, but also accuses him of illicitly executing Arab tribesmen who had accepted Islam—namely members of the Banu Jadhima during the lifetime of Muhammad, and Malik ibn Nuwayra during the Ridda Wars—and being responsible for moral and fiscal misconduct in the Levant. Khalid's military fame disturbed some of the pious early Muslims, most notably Umar, who feared it could develop into a personality cult. Despite attempts in the early sources to discredit Khalid, his reputation has developed as "Islam's most formidable warrior" during the eras of Muhammad, Abu Bakr and the conquest of Syria. Khalid is considered a war hero by Sunni Muslims, while many Shia Muslims view him as a war criminal for his execution of Malik ibn Nuwayra and immediate marriage of his widow, in contravention of the traditional Islamic bereavement period.

Ibn Rushd (4 April 1126 – 11 December 1198), Latinized as Averroes, was a Muslim Andalusian polymath and jurist who wrote about many subjects, including philosophy, theology, medicine, astronomy, physics, psychology, mathematics, Islamic jurisprudence and law, and linguistics. The author of more than 100 books and treatises, Being described as "founding father of secular thought in Western Europe", his philosophical works include numerous commentaries on Aristotle, for which he was known in the western world as The Commentator and Father of rationalism. Ibn Rushd also served as a chief judge and a court physician for the Almohad Caliphate. Averroes was a strong proponent of Aristotelianism; he attempted to restore what he considered the original teachings of Aristotle and opposed the Neoplatonist tendencies of earlier Muslim thinkers, such as Al-Farabi and Avicenna. He also defended the pursuit of philosophy against criticism by Ashari theologians such as Al-Ghazali. Averroes argued that philosophy was permissible in Islam and even compulsory among certain elites. He also argued scriptural text should be interpreted allegorically if it appeared to contradict conclusions reached by reason and philosophy. In Islamic jurisprudence, he wrote the Bidāyat al-Mujtahid on the differences between Islamic schools of law and the principles that caused their differences. In medicine, he proposed a new theory of stroke, described the signs and symptoms of Parkinson's disease for the first time, and might have been the first to identify the retina as the part of the eye responsible for sensing light. His medical book Al-Kulliyat fi al-Tibb, translated into Latin and known as the Colliget, became a textbook in Europe for centuries.

Andrea Doria (1466–1560) was one of the most prominent admirals of the Renaissance, earning a reputation as a formidable naval commander in the Mediterranean. Born in the Republic of Genoa, he initially served under various Italian states before aligning himself with Charles V, the Holy Roman Emperor, in the early 16th century. Doria’s naval prowess was instrumental in securing Genoese independence from French control, and his fleet played a key role in protecting Christian territories from Ottoman incursions. His reforms in naval warfare, including the modernization of Genoa’s fleet and the strategic use of galleys, established him as one of the most influential admirals of his time, shaping maritime conflicts in Europe for decades.

Beyond his military achievements, Andrea Doria was a significant political figure in Genoa, reshaping the city’s governance and securing its autonomy. After expelling the French in 1528, he restructured the republic’s government, ending the dominance of old noble factions and establishing a new oligarchic system that stabilized Genoa’s political landscape. His reforms ensured that Genoa remained a strong and independent maritime republic, closely aligned with Spain but maintaining a degree of sovereignty. Despite being offered titles and lands by Charles V, Doria remained focused on Genoese interests, ensuring that his homeland would not fall under foreign domination. His political influence extended well beyond Genoa, as he played a crucial role in the balance of power between European states.

As a commander in the service of Christian powers, Doria also played a major role in spreading Christianity through naval conquest, particularly by battling Islamic powers in the Mediterranean. He led numerous campaigns against the Ottoman Empire and the Barbary corsairs, capturing key Islamic strongholds and liberating Christian slaves. One of his most notable campaigns was the conquest of Koroni and Patras in Greece, which helped curb Ottoman influence in the region. Through these victories, he not only strengthened Christian control over crucial ports but also facilitated the forced conversion of Islamic populations in these cities. His naval conquests were part of the broader Christian-Muslim struggle in the Mediterranean, reinforcing the religious and political dominance of Christendom in an era marked by conflict between the Ottoman and European powers.

Alexander Hamilton (January 11, 1755 or 1757 – July 12, 1804) was an American statesman, politician, legal scholar, military commander, lawyer, banker, and economist. He was one of the Founding Fathers of the United States. He was an influential interpreter and promoter of the U.S. Constitution, as well as the founder of the nation's financial system, the Federalist Party, the United States Coast Guard, and the New York Post newspaper. As the first secretary of the treasury, Hamilton was the main author of the economic policies of George Washington's administration. He took the lead in the federal government's funding of the states' debts, as well as establishing the nation's first two de facto central banks, the Bank of North America and the First Bank of the United States, a system of tariffs, and friendly trade relations with Britain. His vision included a strong central government led by a vigorous executive branch, a strong commercial economy, government-controlled banks, support for manufacturing, and a strong military. Hamilton's policies as Secretary of the Treasury greatly affected the United States government and still continue to influence it. His constitutional interpretation, specifically of the Necessary and Proper Clause, set precedents for federal authority that are still used by the courts and are considered an authority on constitutional interpretation. The prominent French diplomat Charles Maurice de Talleyrand, who spent 1794 in the United States, wrote, "I consider Napoleon, Fox, and Hamilton the three greatest men of our epoch, and if I were forced to decide between the three, I would give without hesitation the first place to Hamilton", adding that Hamilton had intuited the problems of European conservatives.

Billy Mitchell, remembered as the “father of the United States Air Force,” was a visionary and polarizing figure whose relentless advocacy for airpower reshaped military thinking but ended his career in disillusionment. Born in Nice, France, in 1879 while his parents were on holiday, Mitchell joined the U.S. Army during the Spanish-American War and later served in the Philippines under the command of a young Douglas MacArthur. Rising through the ranks of the Signal Corps, he encountered the fledgling technology of the airplane and became an early and fervent believer in its potential. During World War I, Mitchell commanded the air wing of the American Expeditionary Force, leading thousands of aircraft in offensive operations and earning widespread fame and accolades. Convinced that airpower would revolutionize warfare, he advocated for an independent air service, free from subordination to the Army and Navy, and envisioned airplanes as decisive instruments of war capable of striking deep into enemy territory.

From the perspective of military action, Billy Mitchell was a competent and bold commander, though his brilliance was often overshadowed by his rebellious temperament. He distinguished himself early in his career during the Spanish-American War and in the Philippines, showcasing a solid grasp of conventional military operations. During World War I, Mitchell proved his mettle as a wartime leader, commanding the American Expeditionary Force’s air wing with vision and effectiveness. He orchestrated large-scale air campaigns involving thousands of planes, demonstrating a keen understanding of the strategic and tactical potential of airpower in modern warfare. Mitchell’s ability to inspire enthusiasm among his pilots, coupled with his willingness to push boundaries, made him a formidable force on the battlefield. However, his tendency to disregard protocols and his fiery rhetoric often alienated peers and superiors, limiting his ability to fully integrate his ideas into the military hierarchy. Despite these flaws, his operational successes and forward-thinking strategies underscored his competence as a soldier and commander.

Mitchell’s fiery rhetoric and unorthodox actions repeatedly placed him at odds with the military establishment. In 1921, he orchestrated a dramatic demonstration of airpower by sinking the German battleship Ostfriesland in defiance of carefully laid testing plans, enraging the Navy but captivating public and press alike. His relentless criticism of military leadership, especially after air disasters like the loss of the airship USS Shenandoah, led to his court martial in 1925 for insubordination. Though hailed as a hero by the public, Mitchell was stripped of rank, command, and pay, prompting his resignation from the Army. He continued to champion airpower as a civilian but faded from prominence. Mitchell died in 1936, just before World War II validated his visionary ideas. Today, his legacy endures as both a hero and a heretic who was ahead of his time.

While Bering is not known for engaging in naval battles, his contributions to Russian exploration and the expansion of geographical knowledge in the Pacific region were crucial. Afonso de Albuquerque, often referred to as the "Great Conqueror" or the "Lion of the Seas," was a prominent Portuguese naval commander and statesman during the Age of Discovery. Born in 1453 in Alhandra, near Lisbon, he played a pivotal role in establishing the Portuguese colonial empire in the Indian Ocean. Albuquerque's career is marked by his strategic vision to control key maritime trade routes and his relentless efforts to build a Portuguese stronghold in the East. In 1503, he first set sail for India, participating in the early Portuguese expeditions, but his significant impact began after his appointment as the second governor of Portuguese India in 1509. Albuquerque's aggressive military campaigns led to the capture of strategic locations like Goa in 1510, which became the capital of Portuguese India, and Malacca in 1511, securing control over the vital spice trade. He also attempted to control the Red Sea by capturing Aden and secured the Persian Gulf by capturing Hormuz.

Albuquerque's administration was marked by his visionary policies, aiming to dominate the spice trade and ensure Portuguese supremacy over the Indian Ocean. He was not only a skilled military leader but also a shrewd administrator. He implemented a system of fortified outposts to protect Portuguese interests, promoted intermarriage between Portuguese soldiers and local women to strengthen ties, and established a legal and administrative framework that laid the foundations for the Portuguese colonial empire in Asia. Despite his successes, Albuquerque's methods were often brutal, involving ruthless tactics to subdue resistance, which earned him both respect and enmity. His legacy is a complex one; he is celebrated for his role in expanding Portuguese influence and shaping the course of global trade but also criticized for the harshness of his conquests. Albuquerque died in December 1515, near Goa, shortly after being removed from his governorship, yet his influence endured, leaving an indelible mark on the history of European colonialism in Asia.

Philibert de l'Orme (c. 1514–1570) was a celebrated French architect of the Renaissance, renowned for his innovative designs and role in shaping the architectural landscape of 16th-century France. Born in Lyon, de l'Orme studied in Rome, where he absorbed classical principles that profoundly influenced his architectural philosophy. His career gained momentum under the patronage of King Francis I and his successor Henry II, for whom he worked extensively. De l'Orme's mastery of geometry, symmetry, and the blending of classical and French Gothic styles distinguished him as a visionary architect. He is perhaps best remembered for his work on grand châteaux, which showcased his creative genius and set new standards in French Renaissance architecture

One of de l'Orme's most famous projects was Château de Chenonceau, where he contributed to the design of the bridge that extends across the Cher River, blending functionality with stunning aesthetic appeal. He was also instrumental in the design of Château d'Anet, built for Diane de Poitiers, Henry II's mistress. Château d'Anet exemplified de l'Orme’s architectural philosophy, with its harmonious proportions, innovative use of classical orders, and integration of gardens with the overall structure. Beyond these notable châteaux, de l'Orme also penned architectural treatises such as Le Premier Tome de l'Architecture, which articulated his theoretical approach and influenced subsequent generations of architects. Despite his turbulent later years, including falling out of royal favor, de l'Orme’s legacy endures as a pioneer who redefined French château architecture during the Renaissance

Christopher Clavius (1538–1612) was a German Jesuit mathematician and astronomer, renowned for his role in advancing mathematical sciences during the late Renaissance. A prominent figure in the Gregorian calendar reform of 1582, Clavius was instrumental in devising its mathematical framework, ensuring the calendar's astronomical accuracy and alignment with the solar year. His extensive writings, including "Commentary on the Sphere of Sacrobosco", served as foundational texts in mathematics and astronomy for generations, integrating Ptolemaic traditions with emerging scientific ideas. Clavius also championed the use of mathematical tools in education, significantly contributing to the standardization of mathematical notation and promoting its practical applications in navigation, engineering, and timekeeping.

Clavius’s influence extended deeply into the Jesuit Order, shaping its educational philosophy and positioning mathematics and the sciences as integral to Jesuit pedagogy. As a professor at the Roman College (Collegio Romano), Clavius restructured the curriculum, emphasizing rigorous scientific inquiry alongside traditional theological studies. This model was adopted across Jesuit institutions worldwide, solidifying their reputation as leading centers of education. His efforts helped create a generation of scientifically literate clergy and scholars, enabling the Jesuits to engage effectively with the broader intellectual currents of the era. Clavius’s legacy within the Order reflects his belief in the compatibility of faith and reason, setting a precedent for the Jesuits' long-standing commitment to scientific and intellectual excellence.

Jan Adriaanszoon Leeghwater (1575–1650) was a Dutch engineer, millwright, and innovator, best known for his contributions to land reclamation and water management in the Netherlands. Born in De Rijp, North Holland, Leeghwater grew up in a region that constantly battled rising waters. Harnessing his ingenuity, he became instrumental in the creation of polders—tracts of land reclaimed from water and protected by dikes. Leeghwater played a leading role in projects that drained large lakes, including the Beemster, Purmer, and Schermer, turning once-flooded areas into fertile farmland. These efforts were made possible by his innovations in windmill technology, which provided the power needed to pump water out of low-lying regions.

Leeghwater’s expertise and organizational skills left a lasting mark on Dutch waterworks. He published his seminal work, Het Haarlemmermeerboek (1641), in which he detailed methods for controlling water and maintaining polders. His vision also extended to the ambitious project of draining the Haarlemmermeer (later realized in the 19th century). Leeghwater’s contributions reflect the ingenuity and perseverance that have shaped the Netherlands into a global leader in water management. His legacy endures in the productive lands he helped create and the innovative spirit he embodied, inspiring future engineers to continue the battle against encroaching waters.

Bon da Malamocco, a Venetian merchant with a reputation for boldness and cunning, played a central role in one of the most audacious acts of smuggling in the history of Christendom: the relocation of Saint Mark’s relics from Alexandria to Venice in 828 AD. Bon, along with his accomplice Rustico da Torcello, was sent to the Muslim-ruled city on a mission disguised as a commercial enterprise. Posing as traders dealing in spices and textiles, they befriended the Christian monks guarding the saint’s relics and convinced them that the tomb of Saint Mark was at risk of desecration. Persuasive and charismatic, Bon assured the monks that Venice, a rising power in the Adriatic, would honor and protect the relics in perpetuity. His words bore the weight of both truth and guile, for while Venice sought spiritual prestige, the endeavor was also steeped in a desire for civic pride and political influence.

The actual smuggling was as dramatic as it was sacrilegious. To avoid detection by the Muslim authorities, Bon and his companions concealed the saint’s relics beneath layers of pork and cabbage—an effective ruse, as the Muslim customs officials, forbidden by their faith from handling swine, recoiled at the stench and let the cargo pass unchecked. This ingenious ploy, Bon would later recount with wry satisfaction, was a testament to Venetian wit. Sailing back to the lagoon city, Bon was hailed as a hero upon his return. The relics of Saint Mark were enshrined in what would become the iconic Basilica di San Marco, cementing Venice’s place as a spiritual and mercantile hub. Bon’s name, though often overshadowed by the grandeur of the saint’s resting place, endures as a figure whose daring enterprise forever altered the destiny of his city.
